I don't really have those constant worries about things like money, health, or family; it is almost entirely about my appearance and how it's holding me back.\n\nDoctor: When you worry about your face, do you also spend a lot of time checking mirrors, comparing your appearance to others, or trying to hide or fix the way you look?\n\nPatient: Yes, it's really embarrassing, but I spend 20 to 30 minutes in the mirror before work tilting my head, pulling my skin back, and trying different makeup and lighting. I also take and delete dozens of selfies to check how I'll look on camera, and I constantly ask my husband if I look too old.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe there is actually something wrong with your face that others can clearly see, or do you think the worry may be exaggerated?\n\nPatient: To me, it feels completely real and obvious that my face is sagging and looks wrong, especially around my mouth and eyes, even though my husband and clients try to reassure me. I truly believe it looks that way, and I'm terrified my coworkers and boss will see it and think I'm just too worn out to be taken seriously as a leader.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been able to consider that your face might actually look normal, or are you completely certain that it is truly deformed or wrong despite what others tell you?\n\nPatient: Even though my husband and long-term clients constantly reassure me that I look fine, it is incredibly difficult to believe them. When I look in the mirror, I am completely convinced that my face looks aged, sagging, and just wrong. I find it almost impossible to see it any other way, no matter what they say.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any other unusual beliefs, such as feeling that people are spying on you, talking about you, or trying to harm you, outside of concerns about your appearance?\n\nPatient: No, I have never felt like anyone is spying on me, trying to harm me, or talking about me in that way. My worries are strictly focused on how aged and wrong my face looks, and nothing else like that has ever crossed my mind.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought your face was actually being changed or damaged by an outside force, or is your concern only that it looks unattractive or aged to you and others?\n\nPatient: No, I've never thought any outside force was changing or damaging my face. My concern is strictly that it looks too old, sagging, and worn out to me and others, which makes me feel like no one will take me seriously as a leader at work.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your face is truly deformed or damaged, or could it be that the way it looks is being exaggerated in your mind?\n\nPatient: When I look in the mirror, the sagging and deep lines feel completely real and obvious, as if my face has just collapsed. Even though my husband and clients reassure me, it is incredibly hard to believe them because what I see is so distressing. It really doesn't feel like an exaggeration to me at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered that your face might actually look normal and that this concern could be exaggerated, or are you completely certain that it is truly deformed or wrong despite what others tell you?\n\nPatient: While my husband and clients constantly reassure me that I look fine, I find it incredibly difficult to believe them. When I look in the mirror, the sagging and deep lines look so real and obvious that I am convinced my face looks wrong and too worn out. It is just really hard for me to see it any other way, no matter what they tell me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought that this facial problem might not be real and could be just a worry or exaggeration, or are you completely certain that your face is truly deformed?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure anymore. Deep down it feels completely real and obvious to me, but sometimes I do wonder why everyone else seems to see something different.\n\nDoctor: When you think about your face, do you ever recognize that the concern might be a false belief or a symptom of an illness, or do you feel completely certain it is truly deformed despite what others say?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to answer that, because I've never thought of this as a false belief or an illness. All I know is that when I look in the mirror, the flaws feel completely real and incredibly distressing to me. It is just very hard for me to see it any other way.\n\nDoctor: When you worry about your face, do you ever think there is a chance your belief could be wrong, or are you completely certain that your face is truly deformed or damaged despite what others say?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure how to answer that. While I hear the reassurances from my husband and others, it feels incredibly real to me when I look in the mirror, and I haven't really thought about whether I could be completely wrong.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever think your concern about your face might be a symptom of a mental health condition or an overreaction, or are you completely convinced that your face is truly deformed or wrong?\n\nPatient: I'm here because a nurse I trust urged me to seek help and I know this is hurting my career, but it's still so hard to believe it's just a mental health issue or an overreaction. My concerns are strictly focused on my appearance and how it's impacting my career.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your concern about your face could be a false belief or a symptom of a mental health condition, or are you completely certain that your face is truly deformed or wrong despite what others say?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't know if this is a mental health issue or just reality, and it's very confusing to think about. To me, the flaws on my face feel completely real and are so hard to ignore, even though I am here seeking help.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period when you were completely convinced that your face was deformed or damaged and could not be persuaded otherwise, even for a while? For the most part, the worry just feels very constant and real to me. I don't know if I've had distinct periods of doubt or absolute certainty; it's just always been a struggle.\n\nDoctor: When you think about your face, do you ever recognize that this concern might be a symptom of a mental health condition or an overreaction, or are you completely convinced that your face is truly deformed or wrong despite what others say?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure. To me, my face genuinely looks wrong and too aged, but since a nurse I trust suggested I get help, I am trying to be open to the possibility that I might be overreacting.\n\nDoctor: When you think about your face, do you feel completely certain it is truly deformed or damaged, or can you recognize that this might be a false belief or an overreaction at least sometimes?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to answer that because even though my husband tells me it's not that bad, when I look in the mirror, I feel completely convinced that my face looks terribly aged and wrong. It is just so hard to shake that feeling, even for a second, because what I see looks so real.\n\nDoctor: When you think about your face, do you ever realize that the belief might be exaggerated or untrue, or are you completely convinced it is really deformed even when others disagree?\n\nPatient: It's hard to say.
